title: Maximum in an Array
directAnswer: Initialise `max` to `nums[0]` (never to 0 — that breaks on all-negative arrays) and scan once, updating `max` whenever an element is larger.

remember.takeaway: Seed running extremes with the first element, never a constant.
remember.formula: max = nums[0]; for x in nums: if x > max: max = x
whenToUse: The base step of any running-extreme scan
antiSignals: Array is sorted — the max is just the last element

problemStatement: Given a non-empty integer array `nums`, return the largest element.
understanding: Keep a running maximum: start it at the first element and update it whenever you find something bigger.

approaches.name: Running maximum
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Finding the largest element is the canonical **running maximum** (a 'fold'): carry a best-so-far value and update it whenever you meet something bigger. One pass, constant extra space.

**Why seed with `nums[0]`, never 0.** The accumulator must start at a value that is actually achievable. If you seed `max = 0` and the array is all-negative (e.g. [-5, -1, -8]), nothing ever beats 0, so you'd wrongly return 0 — a value that isn't even in the array. Seeding with the first element guarantees the answer is a real element.

**Why one pass is optimal.** You cannot know the maximum without looking at every element at least once (any element you skip could be the largest), so O(n) is a hard lower bound — there's no cleverer algorithm.

This fold is the atom of `max-of-three`, `second-largest`, Kadane's maximum subarray, and countless other scans. Master the seed-and-update shape here.
hints: Carry a 'best so far' as you walk the array — what should it start as?
Seed it with nums[0], not 0, so all-negative arrays still work.
Update best whenever the current element is larger; one pass is enough.
approaches.insight: Seeding with 0 instead of nums[0] is the classic bug — it returns 0 for an all-negative array.
approaches.complexityReasoning: every element is visited once with O(1) work, and you can't find the max without seeing each element at least once.

java.explanation: Seed with the first element so negatives work.

edgeCases.behavior: Returns -1; seeding with nums[0] (not 0) is what makes this correct.

Starting the scan at index 1 but seeding with 0 instead of nums[0].

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If so I'd return a sentinel or throw; here it's guaranteed non-empty so I seed with nums[0].

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Seeding the max with 0
commonMistakesDetailed.why: For an all-negative array nothing exceeds 0, so you return 0 — a value not in the array.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int max = 0;
for (int x : nums) if (x > max) max = x;   // [-5,-1] -> 0 (WRONG)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int max = nums[0];
for (int x : nums) if (x > max) max = x;
